verses.1: A song. A psalm for the dedication of the house. Of David.
verses.2: I will exalt you, O LORD, because you have rescued me. You did not let my enemies rejoice over me.
verses.3: O LORD my God, I cried out to you and you healed me.
verses.4: O LORD, you brought my soul up from Sheol, you delivered me from the pit of death.
verses.5: Sing to the LORD, you his faithful ones, and give thanks to the memory of his holiness.
verses.6: For his anger is brief, but life is in his favor. In the evening, weeping may stay the night, but in the morning, rejoicing comes.
verses.7: And I said in my complacency, "I will never waver."
verses.8: O LORD, in your favor you made my strength like a mountain. But you turned your face away, and I was terrified.
verses.9: To you, O LORD, I will cry out. To my Lord, I will entreat.
verses.10: What profit is there in my blood, as I descend into ruin? Can the dust praise you? Can it declare your truth?
verses.11: Hear me, O LORD, and be gracious to me. O LORD, be my helper.
verses.12: You turned my mourning into dancing for me. You tore my sackcloth and clothed me with joy.
verses.13: That my glory may sing praise to you, and not be silent. O LORD my God, I will praise you forever.

notes:
Notes
- v. 10: The phrase "What profit is there in my blood" reflects the Hebrew "מה-בטיע בدمי", which metaphorically asks what good is my life/essence in death. The translation seeks to preserve both the rhetorical and emotional weight.
- v. 13: The rendering of "my glory" for "כבוד" is contextually appropriate here, as it refers to the speaker's restored honor or inner joy.
raw:
[1] A song. A psalm for the dedication of the house. Of David.

[2] I will exalt you, O LORD, because you have rescued me. You did not let my enemies rejoice over me.

[3] O LORD my God, I cried out to you and you healed me.

[4] O LORD, you brought my soul up from Sheol, you delivered me from the pit of death.

[5] Sing to the LORD, you his faithful ones, and give thanks to the memory of his holiness.

[6] For his anger is brief, but life is in his favor. In the evening, weeping may stay the night, but in the morning, rejoicing comes.

[7] And I said in my complacency, "I will never waver."

[8] O LORD, in your favor you made my strength like a mountain. But you turned your face away, and I was terrified.

[9] To you, O LORD, I will cry out. To my Lord, I will entreat.

[10] What profit is there in my blood, as I descend into ruin? Can the dust praise you? Can it declare your truth?

[11] Hear me, O LORD, and be gracious to me. O LORD, be my helper.

[12] You turned my mourning into dancing for me. You tore my sackcloth and clothed me with joy.

[13] That my glory may sing praise to you, and not be silent. O LORD my God, I will praise you forever.

---
Notes
- v. 10: The phrase "What profit is there in my blood" reflects the Hebrew "מה-בטיע בدمי", which metaphorically asks what good is my life/essence in death. The translation seeks to preserve both the rhetorical and emotional weight.
- v. 13: The rendering of "my glory" for "כבוד" is contextually appropriate here, as it refers to the speaker's restored honor or inner joy.
